title: Short notation
goal: How keymux, lyk and this site write a stroke for people, and how lyk's dictionary keys are spelled: a group of keys whose sound the generator recorded as the standard letter for it, every other stroke as raw keys; and how both forms are read back.

blocks.x: **A group of keys is written as one symbol only where its split is known.** The generator records, as it writes each outline, which keys wrote which of its word's sounds ([how](#/ref/notation/how-the-split-is-recorded)), and the dictionary files spell every outline whose split is known in this notation, so the key itself is the split: [[night|TPHAOEUT]] is `NĪT`, [[flower|TPHROUR]] (folded) `FLOUR`, [[nature|TPHAEUFP]] `NĀČ`, [[much|UFP]] (a brief the rules write) `UČ`, [[narrates|TPHRA*EUTS]] (a short form, its `TPHR` the N and R it is) `NRĀ*TS`, [[notation|TPHAEUGTS]] (its `T` struck inside the `-GS` of the *shun* it comes before) `NĀTŠN`, [[seems|SAOEPLS]] (Plover's brief, the rules' `SAOEPLZ` with its `-Z` struck `-S`) `SĒMS`. Every other stroke is written raw, a key each, because a guess at its split could be wrong: [[enemy|TPHAEPL]] (a brief whose `AE` writes no vowel lyk's tables know) stays `TPHAEPL`. Input takes both forms.

items: **Each group is written once, in steno order**: a hand's groups by their lowest key, the vowel chord by its mark. That is the order the keys are struck in, so the text names the keys as the hand finds them.

**A single key is its own letter, whatever sound it writes**: the `-S` of *seems* writes its *z* and is `S` (`SĒMS`), the `-D` of a past tense that sounds *t* is `D`, the `-G` of *-ing* is `G`, the `-F` of *have* is `F`. A symbol names a group of keys, never a sound one key happens to make.
**A chord of several keys is its symbol** where the table has one (`-PB` `N`, `-GS` `ŠN`), else the letters of the sounds it writes (`-FT` for *st*: `ST`), else its keys as the table reads them.

**A chord struck around another** (its keys on both sides of a key of another group: `-GS` around the `-T` of *notation*) is written as the cluster symbol of the two together where there is one (`-GTS` `TŠN`, so `NĀTŠN`, the sounds in the order they are said); with none, each group by its lowest key (the outer one first).

**Reading never depends on the order**: a hand's text is read as a set of tokens, each a set of keys, so `NĀTŠN` and `NĀŠNT` are the same stroke. A spelling that would read back as other keys is not used: the outline is written raw.

blocks.x: `build` writes every dictionary key in this notation where the outline's split is known (`"NĪT": "night"`, `"NRĀ*TS": "narrates"`, `"FLOUR": "flower"`) and raw where it is not (`"-S": "yes"`): the key's spelling is the split, so no list of known outlines ships beside the files. `.keymux-notation.json` holds only the symbol table and `"spelled": "keys"`, which tells keymux to read the keys of the dictionaries beside it with the table (a 4 KB file). `build` checks that every key reads back as exactly its outline, raw notation first, and that no two keys read as one outline; keymux and the tools read the keys the same way (see [build and files](#/ref/build-and-files/the-dictionary-files)).

items: **Why.** What a stroke is written as and what the dictionary says it is are one thing: a learner reading a file, keymux's tape, its lookup, its keyboard diagram and this site all show the key as written, and nothing has to be kept in step beside it.

**Plover cannot read the files as they are**: it knows raw notation only. `lyk build --raw` writes every key raw (`TPHAOEUT`), for Plover or any program that needs Plover's notation. typeladder's `lyk.codes.json` stays raw (it is written from the dictionary in memory, not from the files; typeladder would need the symbol table to read short keys).

**Stays raw**: the reserved-stroke files (`01-lyk-commands.json`, `03-lyk-punctuation.json`, `04-lyk-emilys-modifiers.json`, hand-written), the name lane (`03-lyk-names*.json`: its outlines are not recorded yet), a brief whose keys are not its sounds, and `build --raw`.

blocks.x: One character where a standard one exists (dictionary respelling, IPA or established spelling), else the usual dictionary respelling in capitals. A group is written in its hand's colour as one piece. The **source** column says where each symbol comes from; *base* chords are the `[onset]` and `[coda]` of `rules/plover.toml`, *cluster* chords are fixed in `src/notation.rs` (`CLUSTERS`), *measured* ones are chosen by `build` (see [how they were chosen](#/ref/notation/how-the-split-is-recorded)); the counts are strokes lyk wrote from sounds.

blocks.x: The tables list the symbols a learner meets most; `build` measures more for longer runs the same way (150 symbols in all, such as `STK` `DS` for *dis-* and `-FRT` `STR`), all in `.keymux-notation.json`, and `lyk build --report` prints every run's splits. Every other key is its own letter. A run of keys is read from its lowest key: the group with the most keys that starts there, whose keys are all down and with no other key still to write inside its span (`SR` `V` is never read inside `STR`), else the key's own letter. `#` strokes are `#` and letters (`#TR-RL`), never Plover's digits.

A vowel chord is always one sound in lyk (one stroke, one syllable, one vowel), so no outline is an exception for its vowel keys: the mark names the chord. **The star follows the mark**: `AO*EU` is `Ī*` (`NĪ*T`); with no mark the vowel keys and star are as they are, in steno order (`A*`, `*E`), and `EU` with the star is `I*`.

items: **Raw first.** Text that is exactly the raw notation of the keys it parses to is raw (`TPHAEPL`, `ORB`, `P-L`).

**Then short.** `+`, `~` and `#` anywhere (each once); the left hand up to the first vowel symbol, vowel key, star or `-`; the vowel part (marks, vowel keys, the star, at most one `-`, each key once, any order: `Ī*` and `*Ī` both read); then the right hand. Each part is read greedily, longest symbol first. So `NAEM` is `TPHAEPL`, `PL` is `PHR` (P and L), `FLĪT` is `TPHRAOEUT`.
**ASCII** where it reads no other keys: `SH` for `Š`, `CH` for `Č`, `ZH` for `Ž`, `NG` for `Ŋ`, `TH` for `Þ`, `OO` for `Ʊ` (`WISH` is `WEURB`, `BOOK` is `PWAOBG`).
**Then raw, leniently.** Anything else that parses as keys.
An outline written its own way is read back whole first; spaces around a `/` are ignored.

blocks.x: The same rules in `src/notation.rs` (lyk), `site/js/notation.js` (this site) and keymux's `steno/notation.rs`: `lyk lookup NAEM`, `lyk stroke flīt`, keymux's `steno lookup` and this site's Lookup all take either.

items: **lyk.** `lookup`/`keys`/`resolve` (lyk's column only, each group coloured by hand; dim for a solver read), `explain`, `quote`, `paths`, `family`, `ergonomics` (with the keys beside a short form), `mistakes` (the report; the tape is read in either form), `verify-lookup`, `build --report` and `solve --tape`. All through one function, `notation::outline`, reading the symbol table in `out/lyk/.keymux-notation.json` and the spelled keys of the dictionary files beside it, a backup's as a lookup reads it (before any build: the built-in rules' table, every stroke raw).
**This site.** Chips, tables, Lookup and the hover board's label (`data/notation.json`: the same table, and the spelled keys of the outlines the site shows, by their raw outline).

**keymux.** Reads the dictionary keys with the file `deploy` ships beside them, and writes each outline as its key spells it: the tape (overlay and file), the live lookup, `{:outline:...}` and the keyboard diagram; without the file everything is Plover's notation. The diagram draws every key on its own unless the stroke's split is known; a known group lights as one block labelled with its symbol (`Ī` across the four thumb keys, `Š` over `-RB`), the star beside it.

**Stays raw** (read by programs): typeladder's `lyk.codes.json`, the name lane files, the solver plugin, `mistakes --json` and `--drill`, `solve --misses`, the site's `data/` files and page sources (the tools read the dictionary keys back to raw with `tools/notation.py`), and every key `lyk build --raw` writes.

blocks.x: A word the [solver](#/ref/fallback) reads is shown split as the solver read it: keymux asks the plugin's `groups` export right after a reading, and the plugin reads the run again with tracing on (each position in the beam keeps which reading of which stroke it came through), then reports, for each stroke, the chords of two keys or more and the vowel chord that wrote one sound. It costs nothing until keymux asks (the solver's own timing is unchanged: 2 ms a run on average, 6 ms at the 99th percentile), and a report about as much as one fresh reading (2-4 ms). A stroke the reading took whole (a known outline, a suffix chord) has no groups; a run with nothing close enough (the keys read back), a name, a lock or a late star reports nothing, and stays raw. `lyk solve OUTLINE` prints the groups.

The rules write every outline from groups: an onset's runs (`TPH` *n*, `TPHR` *f l*), the vowel (`AOEU` *ay*, with the consonant it takes: `AR`), the coda's runs (`-GS` *sh ən*), a fixed prefix's keys. `build` keeps those groups with every outline it writes (`Rules::outline_split`, `shorten_split`), and carries them through every step that changes an outline after it is written (`src/generate/split.rs`): the join key and the star name no sound, a `-S` respelling or a pinky swap moves its key's sound to the key it moves to, an untypable stroke struck as two takes its groups with it, a marker stroke (`/+*`) has none. A family shape is its root's groups plus the ending's keys (the sounds the member adds), a merged phrase both words' groups, a gold brief the groups of an outline the rules wrote for the word when its keys are that outline by one of those steps (Plover's `SAOEPLS` for *seems*), and a backup join its pieces' strokes as each piece is written. An outline with no record (any other brief, a phrasing-grammar stroke) is attributed with the solver's chord tables as before: each stroke every way its keys can be read as sounds, matched in order against the word's sounds, the cheapest attribution kept, two equally cheap ones that group the keys differently leave it unknown. Over every outline but the backups, each run of two keys or more is counted by how its sounds split; where the commonest split is not how the base symbols read the run, and at least 10 strokes split so, the run gets a symbol of its own (never one that is only its keys' own letters, in any order, nor one another group of that hand already has), and a symbol that would make some run of that hand's keys read back as other keys is dropped, the least used first. `lyk build --report` prints every run's splits and what recording found that the tables could not attribute.

Coverage: 124,004 of the 172,132 generated outlines `deploy` ships (72%) have a known split, up from 97,143 (56%) when the split was only attributed after the build; of the 25,430 briefs, 12,056 are written short. 27,126 shipped outlines are known only because their split was recorded (by what the tables miss in them: a key written for a sound its letter is not 11,724 (`S` as *z* 6,892, `F` as *v* 2,143, `Z` as *s* 1,114, `G` as *ng* 1,088, `T` as *d* 966, `D` as *t* 501, `T` or `D` as *th* 217, `G` as *k* 31), a chord struck around another 5,919, a stroke with no vowel keys 3,954, an attribution the tables found ambiguous 8,497; an outline may count twice).
